fieldMarks: Hairy, brown, black or gray coat
Long pointed head, narrow snout, upright ears and tusks
Long straight tail with a tuft at the tip
Piglets light brown with tan stripes that fade with age
Feral domestic pigs and hybrids can look nearly identical; genetics may be needed to tell them apart
behavior: Lives in family groups called sounders, generally 2–20 animals; adult males often solitary
Breeds from about 6 months old with litters of 2–12, possibly several a year
Roots up the ground while feeding, damaging plants, crops and habitat, and eats ground-nesting birds and other small animals
Quickly learns to avoid people and traps; usually flees rather than fights
habitat: Extreme habitat generalist: forests, swamps, brushlands, grasslands and farmland, preferring to stay near water.
range: Eurasian and North African species. Free-ranging feral swine (wild boar, escaped domestic pigs and hybrids) are reported in at least 35 U.S. states, most commonly in the South, and in Canada mainly in the Prairie Provinces.

lookalikes.name: Feral domestic pig and hybrids
lookalikes.howToTell: Escaped domestic pigs become hairy and grow tusks; visual separation from wild boar is often impossible.
